extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO disciplinary staff, patent attorneys and agents who practice before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and regulatory criteria used by the USPTO/OED to assess practitioner conduct and to approve exclusion on consent; enumerates specific provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and describes factual examples of noncompliance (e.g., third‑party payments, conflicts, withholding filings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to exclude (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32 the USPTO Director has the authority to approve an Affidavit Declaring Consent to Exclusion and to exclude a person from practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides statutory basis for approving consent exclusions; supports publishing disciplinary actions. (Page cites this authority as the basis for the Final Order.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.27 — Consent to exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent submitted an Affidavit Declaring Consent to Exclusion pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.27; the Director reviews and may approve such affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit must comply with § 11.27(a); approval results in exclusion on consent commencing on date of Final Order. (Page: Respondent's affidavit was approved under § 11.27.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.59, 11.60 — Duties during exclusion and reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent acknowledges having read and understood 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.27, 11.58, 11.59, and 11.60 and the legal and factual consequences of consenting to exclusion; upon reinstatement application, OED Director will apply presumptions under § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations include complying with restrictions during exclusion and meeting reinstatement procedures; OED will presume the underlying allegations true for reinstatement review as described in the affidavit and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.102(a) — Consultation obligation / failure to consult
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to consult with clients, inter alia, as required by § 11.104, as to the means by which the objectives of the representation are to be pursued, by, inter alia, not independently advising the USPC-referred clients as to the appropriateness of filing a provisional patent application and, instead, adhering to USPC's instructions to prepare provisional patent applications for USPC-referred clients; by (i) failing to ensure that the $125 fee need not be paid prior to filing; or (ii) not explaining ... that potential adverse consequences may arise under the patent laws (e.g., the AIA's first-inventor-to-file rules) to an inventor's intellectual property rights when the filing ... is withheld or delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative misconduct: deferring to a third party's direction on whether to file, failing to advise independently about provisional vs other filings, and failing to explain timing risks (e.g., AIA first‑inventor‑to‑file consequences) or payment options.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — Diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client by, inter alia, not filing an otherwise ready-to-be-filed provisional patent application for clients ... until receiving instructions from USPC to file the application ... not filing ... until receiving instructions notwithstanding whether the $125 processing fees had been paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: practitioners must pursue client matters diligently and promptly; withholding filing of an otherwise-ready provisional because of third‑party directions or payment conditions violates this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(1) — Informed consent / prompt disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance with respect to which the client's informed consent is required ... by, inter alia, not informing USPC-referred clients that he was required to obtain their informed consent to be compensated by USPC ... failing to inform Client 1 of the conflict between Respondent's interests and Client 1's interests ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must promptly disclose circumstances requiring informed consent (e.g., third‑party payment arrangements, conflicts of interest) and obtain informed client consent before accepting such arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) — Reasonable consultation about means
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished by, inter alia, not explaining ... potential adverse consequences ... (e.g., AIA's first-inventor-to-file rules) ... when the filing of an otherwise ready-to-be-filed provisional patent application is withheld or delayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must consult with client about strategies and means (including timing) so client can make informed decisions; failing to explain statutory timing risks is a breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — Keep client reasonably informed
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter by, inter alia, not informing ... that potential adverse consequences may arise ... not informing ... that (i) the client's otherwise ready-to-be-filed provisional patent application was not being filed because a $125 processing fee had not yet been paid, but need not be paid prior to filing, and (ii) the client may direct TGLG to file his/her ready-to-be filed provisional application and need not wait for USPC ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must keep clients apprised of status and material reasons for delay, including whether third-party payment requirements are controlling and whether clients can direct filing themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — Explanation sufficient for client decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation and keep the client reasonably informed ... by, inter alia, not informing ... of the potential material risks and consequences ... and not informing the clients that their otherwise ready-to-be-filed provisional patent applications were not being filed because the $125 processing fees had not yet been paid, but need not be paid prior to filing ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must explain matters sufficiently for client decisionmaking, including disclosure of why filings are delayed and what clients may do to avoid delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.105(a) — Firm-level reasonable efforts (managerial duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to make reasonable efforts, in his capacity as a partner in a law firm, or as a person possessing comparable managerial authority in a law firm, to ensure that the firm had in effect measures giving reasonable assurance that all practitioners in the firm conformed to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct by, inter alia, not implementing effective measures to ensure that TGLG complied with disclosing to clients the portion of his $2,600 payment to USPC that would be paid to TGLG ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers/partners must implement firm procedures (training, supervision, policies) to ensure compliance with disclosure, fee, and conflict rules; failing to adopt such measures is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b) — Communicate scope and basis of fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to communicate to the client the scope of the representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses for which the client will be responsible by, inter alia, not disclosing to USPC-referred clients the portion of their $2,600 payment to USPC that would be paid to TGLG for referred clients' patent legal services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must disclose scope and fee basis (including portions paid to third parties or referring entities); nondisclosure of fee splits or portions paid to the firm is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a) — Conflicts: significant risk that representation will be materially limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing a client where there is a significant risk that the representation of one or more clients will be materially limited by the practitioner's responsibilities to another client, a former client or a third person or by a personal interest ... deferring to USPC's decision that a provisional application was the appropriate intellectual property protection ... representing clients who owed the $125 fee when the representation involved a concurrent conflict of interest between (i) USPC's interest in collecting the $125 processing fee prior to filing ... and (ii) the client's interest in filing ... to maximize their intellectual property rights ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must avoid or appropriately manage significant conflict risks caused by concurrent duties to third parties (e.g., payors/referrers) that could materially limit client representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a)(2) — Conflicts: material limitation by duties to others (specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing a client where there is a significant risk that the representation ... will be materially limited ... by, inter alia, deferring to USPC's decision that a provisional application was the appropriate IP protection rather than independently counseling USPC-referred clients ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same-theme specific: failing to independently counsel clients (instead deferring to third party preferences) creates a material limitation conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f) — Accepting compensation from third party without informed consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting compensation for representing a client from one other than the client without informed consent, by failing to disclose to USPC-referred clients the portion of their $2,600 payment to USPC, a third party, that would be paid to TGLG and not obtaining the client's informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must disclose and obtain client informed consent before accepting third‑party payments that relate to the representation; nondisclosure is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f)(2) — Third-party payment where independence is interfered
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting compensation for representing a client from one other than the client where there is interference with the practitioner's independence of professional judgment by accepting compensation from USPC and allowing USPC to direct TGLG to file a provisional patent application for the USPC-referred clients without first consulting with the clients as to the best method for protecting the clients' inventions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If third-party payment creates interference with independent judgment (e.g., third party directs selection/timing of filings), the arrangement is impermissible unless properly managed and consented-to.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.110(a) — Representation prohibited when firm member would be barred
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing a client when any member of the firm with which the practitioner is associated would be prohibited from doing so by §§ 11.107 or 11.109 by, inter alia, representing USPC-referred clients while also representing USPC without obtaining informed consent when those Respondent associated with in his firm, his subordinates, in particular his subordinate Patent Practitioner Employee would have been prohibited from doing so under § 11.107 ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may not undertake representation that would be barred for another firm member (e.g., because of conflicts) without resolving those conflicts and obtaining required consents.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(a)(1) — Withdrawal when representation will result in violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing a client, or where representation has commenced, failing to withdraw from the representation if the representation will result in violation of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct or other law by inter alia, representing USPC-referred clients and/or failing to withdraw from the representation thereof while also representing USPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must withdraw if continuing representation will cause a rules violation (e.g., unwaivable conflicts) and should not maintain dual representations that create such violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.201 — Independence of professional judgment and candid advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to exercise independent judgment and render candid advice by, inter alia, deferring to USPC's decision that a provisional application was the appropriate intellectual property protection ... not filing an otherwise ready-to-be-filed provisional patent application ... until receiving instructions from USPC ... withholding the filing ... because a $125 fee had not yet been paid ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must exercise independent judgment and give candid advice to clients; subordinating legal judgment to a third party or conditional payment requirements undermines independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.501(a) — Firm measures to ensure practitioner conformity (firm duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm had in effect measures giving reasonable assurance that all practitioners in the firm conform to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct by inter alia, not implementing effective measures to ensure that TGLG complied with § 11.104(a)(1), § 11.105(b) and § 11.108(f) such that TGLG disclosed to USPC-referred clients the portion of their $2,600 payment to USPC that would be paid to TGLG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firms must adopt policies/procedures to assure compliance (disclosures, supervision, fee communications); failure to do so is firm-level misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.501(b) — Supervisory responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: As a practitioner having direct supervisory authority over another practitioner, failing to make reasonable efforts to ensure that the other practitioner conforms to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct by, as a practitioner who has direct supervisory authority over his subordinate Patent Practitioner Employee, failing to make reasonable efforts to ensure that Respondent's subordinate complied with the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct; not implementing effective measures to ensure that his subordinate employees complied with §§ 11.102(a), 11.103, 11.104(a)(2), 11.104(a)(3), 11.104(b), 11.201, and 11.504(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors must reasonably oversee subordinates and implement measures to ensure compliance; failure to do so can constitute supervisory misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.501(c) — Responsibility for another practitioner's violation (ordering/ratifying/failing to remediate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining responsibility for another practitioner's violation of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct if: (i) the practitioner orders or, with knowledge of the specific conduct, ratifies the conduct involved, or (ii) the practitioner is a partner or has comparable managerial authority ... and knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated but fails to take reasonable remedial action by, inter alia, knowing of and ratifying (by continuing to allow the conduct) Respondent's subordinate Patent Practitioner Employee's conduct ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers/supervisors who know of subordinates' misconduct and fail to act (or who ratify it) bear responsibility; examples include knowing of nondisclosure of fee splits or withholding filings and failing to remediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.504(c) — Permitting third party to direct/regulate professional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting a person who recommends, employs, or pays the practitioner to render legal services for another to direct or regulate the practitioner's professional judgment in rendering such legal services by, inter alia, deferring to USPC's decision that a provisional application was the appropriate intellectual property protection ... deferring to, and waiting for, USPC's decision as to when to file the provisional patent applications ... withholding the filing ... until a $125 fee was paid to USPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not allow payors/referrers to control professional judgment or timing of legal services; allowing a third party to dictate filing decisions is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — Practicing law in violation of another jurisdiction's rules / assisting another
rubrics_metrics.description: Practicing law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction, or assisting another in doing so, by inter alia (i) lending Respondent's firm's implied name and imprimatur ... (ii) knowing that USPC always used the TGLG prior art references and patent search reports to induce the purchase of provisional patent applications; and (iii) knowing that USPC was explaining legal concepts such as provisional patent applications, non provisional applications, and design patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not assist others in unauthorized practice or act in ways that facilitate improper legal service delivery (e.g., lending firm credentials to a nonlawyer vendor inducing legal purchases).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(a) — Violating or assisting violations of the Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Violating or attempting to violate the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct, knowingly assisting or inducing another to do so, or doing so through the acts of another in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad prohibition: participating in, assisting, or inducing rule violations by self or others is misconduct. (Page alleges such conduct.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation by, inter alia, establishing a pattern and practice of informing USPC-referred clients that a $125 processing fee was due prior to the filing of their provisional patent applications, and/or directing Respondent's subordinate Patent Practitioner Employee's to do so, when the $125 was not required prior to filing, and in some instances not required to be paid by the referred clients' contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresenting material facts to clients or using deceptive statements about filing requirements or payments (e.g., misrepresenting need for a $125 pre-filing fee) is misconduct under the dishonesty/fraud provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice requirements (Official Gazette and OED FOIA Reading Room)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at the Office of Enrollment and Discipline's electronic FOIA Reading Room ... and publish a notice in the Official Gazette that is materially consistent with the provided notice of exclusion on consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirement: disciplinary actions and notices of exclusion are to be published electronically and in the Official Gazette with materially consistent content summarizing the action and allegations.
